utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Morning. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Our next witness is General Djordje Curcin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. I believe Mr. Djurdjic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. Would you please kindly introduce yourself for the record and give us your basic personal details.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I was born on the 19th of July, 1945, in Vojvodina, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't hear your full name, though.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Djordje Curcin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, you provided a statement to the Defence team of General Ojdanic on the 24th of August, 2007, and you signed it. Do you stand by that statement given on the 24th of August, 2007?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for the document D006-0405 to be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D00533. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, on the 5th and on the 6th of October, 2007, you testified in the Milutinovic case before this Court. In proofing for today's testimony you reviewed that transcript. Now I have to ask you: If you were asked the same questions today, would you provide the same answer?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I ask for the document D010-0885 under seal to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript of the evidence of the witness in the Milutinovic trial will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be received as Exhibit Number D00556 -- and correction to the previous document, that is document D006-0405 shall be received as Exhibit Number D00553, not 533.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. Let me just say that again on record. The previous document shall be received as Exhibit Number D00553, whilst the later document which is D010-0885 shall be received as D00554 under seal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we also have a redacted version of the transcript, Exhibit D011-2017. I tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It too will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be received as Exhibit Number D00555. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will now present a summary of the statement of General Djordje Curcin. The witness is a colonel-general in the Army of Yugoslavia, now retired. Pursuant to a decree of the president of the FRY on the 28th of December, 1998, he was transferred to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and in the period from 8th to 13th January he assumed the duties of the chief of the first administration in the section for operations and staff affairs of the General Staff. He will give evidence of his experiences and daily operative reports. He supervised and monitored the situation along the state border, and he will share with us his knowledge on the violations of the border regime as well as information that he gleaned from combat reports drawn up by strategic groupings, especially reports of 3rd Army that he studied on a daily basis. The witness will testify that the first administration, as part of their section for operative and staff affairs, represents the staff and is a co-ordination body of the General Staff. He will describe the method of functioning of the General Staff, the section for operations and staff affairs, and the first administration. He will give evidence about his attendance at and the knowledge he had from attending meetings of the General Staff and the Supreme Command during the war. He was involved in drawing up plans, issuing orders and other important documents of the Supreme Command Staff. He will also speak about the level of combat-readiness of the Army of Yugoslavia in the course of 1999. He will speak in greater detail about the method of producing combat reports of the Supreme Command Staff and the reports of the combat groups received by the Supreme Command Staff with an emphasis on the 3rd Army. He will give evidence in particular about the meeting of the General Staff that discussed the plan of preventing the forced arrival into the territory of Kosovo and Serbia of NATO forces. As member of the Supreme Command Staff, he personally was involved in the drawing up of instructions, plans, telegrams, documents, orders, et cetera. The witness will also give evidence about the method of safekeeping of and handling of sensitive documentation, as well as the operation of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, including co-operation with international organisations and monitoring missions. The witness will also tell us that the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the Army of Yugoslavia never had a plan, an order, or any such document that would involve plans to instigate or order or aid and abet crimes and terror against the population of ethnic Albanians in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo. Such plans could never have existed without the knowledge of this witness. The witness will explain to us the command system of the Army of Yugoslavia, the system of reporting along the chain of command, and he will familiarise us with the mobilisation that took place in March 1999. The witness will share with us his knowledge about the training given to the troops of the Army of Yugoslavia on international humanitarian law in 1999 and during the entire aggression. He will explain that the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the Supreme Command Staff applied all the norms governing the knowledge, observation, and application of international governance and international humanitarian law, through workshops and orders of the General Staff and the Supreme Command Staff. The witness will also tell us that the General Staff of the VJ and the Supreme Command Staff always supported the peaceful option in resolving the problem of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell us briefly about all the positions you occupied in your military career?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Upon completing the military academy in Belgrade and Sarajevo, I was first commander of the recruits platoon in Bileca and the instructor in training practice -- in target practice. Then I was company commander, deputy battalion commander, commander of the recruits platoon at the military academy, and tactics instructor to cadets at the military academy. After that I was battalion commander, an operations officer in a brigade, operations officer in a corps, operations officer on army level, and General Staff level. In the meantime, I discharged other duties such as commander of the Guards Motorised Regiment, Motorised Brigade, group of brigades, and some other duties. My last and highest two positions were operations officer in the 1st Army for five and a half years, and just before my retirement, starting with early 1999, I was chief of the first operations administration at the General Staff and the Supreme Command Staff. I was retired on the 30th of September, 2001, in the rank of lieutenant-general or, in Western terms, three-star general.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard that in the beginning of 1999 you joined the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Could you tell us briefly about the organisation of the General Staff at the time when you arrived and about the role played by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The General Staff is the highest professional organ of the Army of Yugoslavia. It's the highest staff and professional organ preparing the army for war. At that time the General Staff had the following organisational units: A section for operations and staff affairs; a section of the ground forces; a section of the navy; air force section; section for recruitment, mobilisation, and replenishment; logistics sector; and independent administration; intelligence administration; administration for morale. Those are the most important units, but there was also the office of the Chief of the General Staff and a section, later administration, for relations with international military representatives and organisations. Those are the main organisational units of the General Staff at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were in the operations and staff sector -- section. Could you tell us briefly about the role of that section, and in particular the assignments of the first administration which you headed.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The operations and staff affairs section had two administrations: The first, operations department; and the second, finance. There was also a section for operations and staff affairs that serviced the chief. I was head of the first administration, but also deputy chief of the operations and staff affairs department. It actually serviced the entire General Staff and the Chief of the General Staff, providing all the necessary documents, evaluations, proposals, et cetera. The first administration ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you want to say something more about the first administration?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the transcript, for the typing to finish. I'll go on. The first administration was also inter-branch and inter-departmental. It had -- it included representatives of all branches and arms of service to be able to service the whole army. It had several organisational units within it. One of them dealt exclusively with planning the employment of the army and other systems. Without that unit, no plan could be made, and that unit kept in a special place all the plans. Then there was another organisational units in charge of combat-readiness of the Army of Yugoslavia. And when I say "Army of Yugoslavia," I mean the command, the entire system, and all branches. There was a section, a unit, for border service because at that time it was the Army of Yugoslavia that secured the state border along its entire length, over 2.000 kilometres, outside of border crossings, and populated areas. In populated areas and at border crossings, the security for the state border was provided by a special organisational unit of the Ministry of the Interior. The administration included several more organisational units, such as the unit for operations and staff affairs, for a survey, land survey, because the land survey institute was subordinated to that unit and they made all the maps. There was also a bookkeeping department, keeping record of all the incoming and outgoing documents of the General Staff. As you can conclude from what I've said so far, this was a very complex organisation with many components, over 60 of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just interested -- we covered the organisation before the war. During the war, just very briefly, were there any changes in the organisational structure in the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, there were. What I just described was the peacetime structure. In the event of war, there was a wartime structure which had been laid down much earlier. Each officer who in that situation, in wartime, received a wartime assignment in the Supreme Command Staff had a special order for that. This is probably a unique example that the General Staff is larger in peacetime than the Supreme Command Staff during wartime. This is for specific reasons, primarily because of the capacity of the command post and the long time required to stay there without going in or out because there was a special procedure for that. So that the size of all the organisational units and the Supreme Command Staff was actually reduced in order for it to be more efficient during its 24-hour work, during the 78 days of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the war, the Supreme Command Staff also changed its name. Did the organisational units also change their names during the war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. This is something that is regulated with the wartime assignment, even though this was not done according to some legal framework. Previously there had been a Supreme Command Staff and a Supreme Command; however, after some changes and the break-up of Yugoslavia, all the laws were not adopted in time. So we worked as if they were because we needed to function in a time when the country was attacked. The organisational units also changed their structure because they were smaller. So, for example, the sector for administration -- the sector became an administration and so on. For example, the sector became the administration for staff and operations affair, while the operations administration became a section. And this is what happened throughout the army in all the other sectors. I also would like to remark that there was some changes made and that independent administrations became parts of former sections. For example, the second intelligence administration became a special sector, became a staff operations administration, and was tightly connected with the operations administration or the operations section. So on the basis of their monitoring the situation, we drafted our orders in order to stream-line our work more. So this was one way. The Chief of the General Staff resolved this by making the appropriate wartime assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to look at Exhibit D179.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would you permit us to provide the witness with a binder containing the hard copies of all the documents in order that we could go through them more efficiently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you can just open up the binder so that you can use the documents. We're looking at tab 1. This is document D179. Sir, we are now looking at the directive for the engagement of the Army of Yugoslavia in order to prevent the forced introduction of a multi-national NATO brigade in KiM. It's dated the 16th of January, 1999. Can you please tell us whether you took part in the drafting of this directive?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I personally participated, and I drafted a part of the -- actually, and some members of the operations administration because this document was being kept there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who else participated in the drafting of this directive?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This directive was drafted by the operations administration and the intelligence administration, the security administration, the counter-intelligence sector, the logistics sector, the electronic and surveillance and counter-surveillance section. It's interesting about how this idea for this directive came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That would be my next question. Can you please tell us why this directive was drafted in early January 1999.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The chief of the intelligence administration, General Krga, when he took up his duties concluded that there was a possible eventuality that we were not prepared for, and he informed the Chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic, about this. And General Ojdanic immediately ordered that a team get together and begin to draft a document in order to prevent such a situation. The gist of it was that there were significant NATO forces in Bosnia and that NATO forces had already began to gather in Greece and then in Macedonia and Albania. We had a large number of terrorist and sabotage actions in Kosovo, and there was a real danger that at one point if the rebellion in Kosovo and Metohija really got going, the forces from Bosnia, Macedonia, and Albania would begin to move simultaneously, and with the rebellion in Kosovo and Metohija growing strong they could cut off that area and create a completely different situation on the ground. In that way they would achieve several objectives, the main of which would be to install NATO forces in Kosovo and Metohija for a prolonged period of time. As can be seen in recent years, they actually did achieve that goal, after ten years or so, with the separation of Montenegro and the secession of Kosovo and the location of their forces for their own purposes. So our estimates and assessments on this matter have proven correct, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 8 in the English version and page 5 in the Serbian version. This is 3.1.3. This is the paragraph that we should be looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So this is page 4 in your binder. Could you please comment on this first phase.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Tasks and then we have 3.1, the 3rd Army. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: By undertaking counter air attack measures, because we did expect some heavy bombing once NATO decided to embark on that, it was essential to provide adequate forces for the protection of the units. And in co-ordination with the air force and anti-aircraft defence, to prevent the arrival of a multi-national brigade from Albania into Kosovo and Metohija. In military terms and the only correct way of proceedings, it was essential to also seal off the axis from where terrorist forces could come from Macedonia and Albania, and also to ensure that all the roads were passable. Besides that, it was also important to achieve or maintain combat control of the territory. The concept was militarily justified and the idea was not to permit the multi-national forces to link up with the hotbeds of rebellion of the Siptar terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us what the nature of this directive was?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: It's clear to any military man - and I hope that it's clear to any person as well - that this is an entirely defensive -- that it is of an entirely defensive nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go back one page, General. Now in your hard copy we would go back to page 3, and in the English it would be page 7. Could you please comment on the combat-readiness in terms of this directive.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: First we specified what a directive was. A directive is issued from the federal level, from the level of the General Staff, for a longer time-period. It's not a daily assignment or one that would take two to seven days. This is a longer-term assignment, in the event of such a situation occurring. The situation may never occur, and the directive may never be applied. This is why we're not talking about readiness here. If we pay attention to the last line, there is no explicit remark on the combat-readiness with a dead-line, but this is something that would be dependent on the decision of the commander of the 3rd Army and the commander of the air force and the anti-aircraft defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at the last page of the document. I think this is page 12 in the English version. In your copy, General, it's page 6. What I'm interested in here is it says "attachment." Could you please explain this a little bit.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, the attachment is the forced engagement of a multi-national NATO brigade in Kosovo and Metohija, map ratio 1:200.000. If we were to have a map here now, everyone would be informed about the nature of the information being -- operation being planned here. Without the map, the text is really insufficient. Perhaps if we could find the map and show it, then we would see the two phases that we are discussing here. So then you could see exactly who would be doing what when, and that no soldier would be actually crossing the borders of Serbia in order to implement the assignments stated in this directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I can see here that you drafted this document. It says here "drafted by Lieutenant-General Djordje Curcin." We have also the distribution list, and it's being distributed to all the strategic groups and some others. What I'm interested in is this: Did the armies have the task of continuing and drafting their own documents pursuant to this directive?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, the answer to your first question is correct. We have the distribution list here, how many copies, which copies were sent to which command also. This document, this directive, is a special type of document. This is a document on the planned use, and it's marked as a state secret. And there is also a code-name, Grom 3, Thunderbolt 3, so it's not a normal kind of order. It's drafted pursuant to a special procedure, and it's kept in a special manner. So other than those who actually drafted it, no one has access to this plan. Each time a plan is used, this is recorded. So on the basis of this directive, all the strategic group commands that received a copy of it were obliged to draft their own orders and certain documents in order -- should the need arise to be able to implement the directive in its entirety. This is something that is done in advance. Another important thing, at all the lower levels they have to maintain the same level of secrecy. It's classified as a state secret. So the classification also has to be kept, Thunderbolt 3. The document was drafted at the army level. I know that it was drafted in the 3rd Army. I did have the opportunity to look at it when it was submitted for evaluation in late January, and on the basis of that plan of the 3rd Army, the plan of the Pristina Corps was developed and then the plans of all the brigade commands after that -- we were informed about that. Yes, yes, just one more sentence. We were informed about that at a Chief of the General Staff collegium in mid-February, and I informed the Chief of the General Staff that this plan was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at document D343 -- Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This would be in tab 2, General, in your binder. This is an order for the use of the 3rd Army, which the command of the 3rd Army issued on the 27th of January, 1999. If you can, can we please look at page 3 of the English version and the Serbian version. General, I would like to ask you to comment on item 2 on that page, the task of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This is now putting into operation what I talked about before based on the decree what I talked about before -- directive that I talked about before. The army command copies, literally, the assignment which they were issued by the General Staff. And you can easily see that because the task was to provide security measures to the adequate forces, and in joint co-operation with the anti-aircraft defence and the air force to prevent the arrival of NATO from Kosovo [as interpreted] and Macedonia to Kosovo and Metohija and to occupy specific facilities in sectors that were relevant. Then we -- equally important we see that their task was to seal off the axes that could be used for the entry of multi-national forces and their equipment. And also, to prevent the linking up of the NATO brigade with the Siptar terrorist forces in Kosovo by taking up actions against the Siptar terrorist forces. This was the primary task.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, you told us a little bit before that on the basis of the instructions of the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps, and units within the Pristina Corps developed the Thunderbolt 3 directive. If you can just briefly tell me, who had access and the right to be informed about a directive in peacetime and wartime, and how could one have access to this plan that was drafted? I'm talking about lower-ranking units, brigades. I'm not thinking of the General Staff here.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I think that I understood your question. At all levels, the access to -- this document is very restricted. People who have access to this kind of plan or orders that are classified as a state secret are very few. Perhaps in passing someone can see remotely something that could be considered a plan, but this plan is drafted in a special way and it is being kept according to a special regime. It's constantly guarded and technical security measures are also in effect. It's being kept in a special vault that cannot be damaged by fire or any other kind of harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The desk officer for the security of the barracks, does he have access to such a plan, or does he have access to the war combat plan?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document D006-0440, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This would be tab 3 in your binder, General. This is a document by the General Staff of the 21st of January, 1999, signed by Lieutenant-General Svetozar Marjanovic, asking the 3rd Army to be deployed in the village of Racak sector. Can you please tell us why this document was sent.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, I know everything about this document. I signed it. At the bottom you can see my initials. In that period, in the media, especially foreign media, there was an attempt to launch the idea by means of propaganda about a crime in Racak in which -- which was perpetrated by the military and the police. This was something that we discussed at the Chief of the General Staff collegium at that time. We reviewed the reports of the 3rd Army command and the Pristina Corps of the 15th, the 16th, and the 17th, and concluded that there was no military engagement there in the Racak sector. However, in order to be absolutely sure, the Chief of the General Staff ordered at the collegium that a special document be sent to the command of the 3rd Army requesting a special extraordinary report and that he should seek a special written report from the commander of the Pristina Corps in order to respond to specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see what is being asked for here. Now, could you please explain, this document, what is it by its form? What sort of a document is it? Is there a code?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This is a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let us take it slowly. I'm going to put questions to you. Maybe we can cover this more quickly. So this is a telegram. Can you please tell us what the usual required form of a telegram would be, like a template at that time in the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Just as you see here, you would have a stamp at the top with a date, and then on the right-hand side would be the code, and then it would state to whom the document should be delivered, either to the commander or to the command. You can see that it's only being sent to the 3rd Army command. There is a brief heading, which here is the interim report. And then below the signature you have the signature of Lieutenant-General Svetozar Marjanovic, and then you have the initials of the person who typed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: And the command that is issuing the document would be stated in the upper left-hand corner, and they are the ones who put the stamp, the date and the number of the -- the document was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. The document that we see is a photocopy. It's not the original. It's a signed document, though. Is that a copy that is kept in the archive of the person or the body sending out the document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me on the basis of this copy, technically, actually, how is it handled? It's a telegram. General Marjanovic signed it and then what happens next? What is the procedure?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I also received it for signature. Once he signed it I dispatched it to the log office. You can see the document was registered by hand, this was not typed. And then the chief of the office took it to the encryption section, he signed for it there -- it was signed for there as well. After the telegram was coded and dispatched and received at the address, the document would then be returned by the person to our archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So, General, the first original copy would have the signature of the author of the telegram?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And now, can you tell me the copy that is being dispatched, does that contain any kind of marking as to the time of dispatch or anything?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The copy that is left for dispatch has to have a rectangular stamp at the bottom, and the stamp would contain its boxes where one would indicate the time of -- it was received in order to be dispatched, the time it was actually dispatched, and the time it was actually received at the destination, and also the date when it was received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We'll see that in the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document shall be received as Exhibit Number D00556. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now ask for D006-0442. It's 41 ter for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is the command of the 3rd Army, 21st January, 1999, sent personally to the Chief of the General Staff. Could you tell us about this document and its format.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This is a telegram from the command of the 3rd Army, a reply to our dispatch of the 21st as well, sent personally to the attention of the Chief of the General Staff who signed the previous telegram. They answer our questions, and once again they assert positively that the army was not involved and they provide details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, turn to page 2, please. Would you explain the two stamps we see below the text.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: On the left-hand side at the bottom we see a stamp that confirms that the telegram was processed at 0430 hours on the 21st. We see a round stamp of the communications centre. This is a telegram outside normal hours, and it arrived therefore at the operations centre, which is open 24/7. And the chief of communications, Colonel Stupic [phoen], noted down that it was received on the 21st of January, and he registered it. You see the reference number here. He did another thing, and that is to make four copies and send them to four addresses: The deputy chief through the head of office, the Chief of Staff, the chief of the section for operations and staff affairs, and the chief of the first administration so that they were all informed before they arrived in Kosovo. This is in fact an inquiry whether the army was involved in Racak or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it normal to send this? Was it normal procedure to send a document like this to four different administrations, at least when documents involving subject matter relevant to several administrations?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. When several administrations need to be informed or need to act upon something, they -- the document is copied to all of them. That avoids complication. Otherwise, one of the recipients would have to do the copying and forwarding and also this provides for unified bookkeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the first administration receives all the telegrams for the General Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't think I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, then explain.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: A telegram is received by the addressee, whoever that may be. But this obviously was a document registered in the first administration, and it relates to the first administration. But it was written for the attention of the Chief of the General Staff, and that's why it was also sent to the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And if something is sent to the Chief of the General Staff, does he have his own reception office, or where do his telegrams arrive?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: All telegrams go to the operations centre and are forwarded from there. There is a special provision that stipulates that in working hours a telegram goes directly to the addressee; however, during the night there is no one there to receive it. So it goes to the operations centre and then the operations centre can contact the addressee to ask them whether they want it forwarded immediately or should it wait for the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And this one, to whom was it addressed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The first operations administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender this document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit Number D00557. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D523.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 5 for you, Witness. It's number 6 on the Defence list. It's an evaluation of the security situation and the threats to the FRY made by the first administration in February 1999. Tab 5, General. Could you tell us why this evaluation was made by your administration. What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I think I've already mentioned that certain new terrorist activities were -- had been carried out by the KLA in Kosovo at that time. The Chief of the General Staff ordered a detailed evaluation be made from the intelligence and security point of view of the current threats to Yugoslavia. I have already said that monthly evaluations were made, but sometimes a more detailed and long-term evaluations were needed. This is one of them, ordered commission by the Chief of the General Staff at one of the collegium meetings. It was produced by a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that later, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at page 23 in English and 21 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In your copy it's page 17, General. It's a proposal of measures. 5.1 and 5.2 are the paragraphs I'm interested in. Comment briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The purpose of this complex inter-disciplinary evaluation was to provide a realistic evaluation of the situation and possible security threats and, finally, to propose measures. What kind of measures? Contingency measures in the event of success and/or failure of the Rambouillet negotiations. Of course for us the situation was graver in the event of failure of these negotiations. We were all anxious for a peaceful solution in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 24 in English and your next page in English, 5.2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the first variant, failure, was the hardest for us. And under 5.2 we proposed measures at the level of the VJ, Army of Yugoslavia, in the event of a peaceful solution, and we listed our tasks in the order of urgency and importance. And I hope that once we've read this we will all see that all these were defensive measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the last page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We see this was produced by a working team, your page 20, General. Page 24 in e-court -- no, it's 24 in English. In Serbian it's -- anyway, we see the team. Who was on that team?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that this was a complex inter-disciplinary exercise and that's why this working team was established. It was headed by assistant Chief of the General Staff for operations and staff affairs, General Obradovic; following by me, as chief of the first administration; there were also chief of the security administration, General Dimitrijevic; assistant Chief of the General Staff for land forces, General Panic; assistant Chief of the General Staff for logistics, General Pantelic; chief of the intelligence administration, Branko Krga; and chief of the administration for information and morale, General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now have P1333. This is a session of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army of 2nd February 1999. We need page 20 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English it's page 19, paragraph 5, in e-court; and in Serbian it's page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: For you, General, it's tab -- it's page 16 in the hard copy. We see your contribution to the discussion, General. Could you just comment on this passage where it says: "We propose that you order to corps commanders and commanders of special units ..." have you found this?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. I think I've already said that I regularly participated in collegium deliberations dealing with the subject matter that was within the jurisdiction of the first administration. Here I presented a couple of proposals, among other things. I suggested to the Chief of the General Staff that we should issue an order that would be binding for corps commanders and commanders of special units and other independent units to perform a drill to check their readiness in the case -- in case of air-strikes. We were expected that a NATO aggression would begin with air-strikes using rockets fired by fighter planes. To prevent being taken by surprise, I suggested drills that would train the units in rapid evacuation of barracks to avoid losses. And we -- I also suggested that in this drill we do not relocate to our real back-up locations because the enemy would certainly note these locations down, but to use other exercise locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now please look at the end, the final passage, in your contribution. In English it's page 20. Just a moment until they zoom in. It's the last paragraph in your contribution.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I took the liberty to think and to propose what I thought was best for the Army of Yugoslavia at the moment. That's what General Ojdanic expected of all the members of the collegium, not to simply say "yes" to whatever he said, but to share their own opinions. This was my personal proposals, namely, to convene a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council and that at least in one part of the meeting army commanders be present so that members of the state leadership could hear them out and at least wonder why commanders of strategic groups were present at the meetings. We thought the situation was very serious and the leadership should know the truth, and this is my proposal to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was such a meeting indeed held?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was ten days later, on the 12th of February, and the supreme commander, President Milosevic, was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D006-0466.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is an aide-memoire for briefing the president of the FRY, and we see the date at the top, 12th February, 1999. To whom was this aide-memoire made and by whom and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This is an aide-memoire for reporting to the president of the FRY, reporting by the Chief of the General Staff. The office of the chief and the first administration were involved in producing this aide-memoire, but also the fifth administration because it involved funds and materiel which was the responsibility of the fifth administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Page 1 of the English should remain, and in Serbian can we turn to page 2. It says this plan became obsolete within just a few months. It's about plans Grom 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Grom 1 and 2 plans were made in July 1998. Since then, a lot had changed. NATO had begun accumulating forces and they had already 9- to 10.000 troops in Macedonia. Second, verifiers had arrived in our territory after October, after the agreement, and the situation in the wider region had also become more complicated. There were aircraft carriers in the Adriatic Sea, over 2- or 3.000 marines and around ten different ships were facing Yugoslavia. The situation was drastically different, and a multi-national brigade had been deployed in Macedonia, ready to move at short notice by helicopter towards Yugoslavia. That was the situation at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D00558. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P1338, page 12 in English and 12 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: For you, Witness, it's tab 8, page 10. Again, your contribution. In English it would be paragraphs 7 and 8. It begins with: "I propose inspection and a tour ..."

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The first administration was in charge of checks and inspections. It planned, organised, wrote orders, and assembled teams from various sections, depending on what the inspection was about. We had an annual and a monthly plan of inspection, but interim inspections were also needed. This was such an extraordinary occasion, where I suggested inspecting units on the borders of Kosovo and Metohija. In fact, under the agreement new forces were banned from entering Kosovo and Metohija, but there was no restriction on deploying units in the border belt of Kosovo and Metohija. Certain forces could be deployed there for the contingency of aggression, and we propose that we organise an inspection of these units. And apart from the units subordinated to us, to our administration, there were also air force and air defence units in reserve there. I suggested postponing the inspection of units in Kosovo and Metohija. Why? Because within a few days we were expecting a contingent of troops mobilised for the 3rd Army, but the chief ordered that they should not be trained in Kosovo, to be an easy target like lay pigeons for the enemy. He ordered that they should be trained within the 2nd Army and those who were specialised for the navy and air force should get training there, within the 3rd Army, and once trained they would be sent to Kosovo with proper notification to the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P1335. It's a session of the collegium of the 4th of March, 1999, page 14 in English and in Serbian that would be page 13 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In your binder it's page 12. Again, this is your discussion and a proposal of measures, 1, 2, and 3. Tell us briefly, please, about these measures you are proposing.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. We've noted analysing previous sessions of the collegium that the main purpose of meeting was to propose specific steps, and that's what I do here. The first suggestion was to implement verbatim the order of the training of soldiers from December the previous year. As I said a moment ago, they were trained for the purposes of the 3rd Army, but in the areas of other groups. They were supposed to be shipped, or rather, transferred by train on the 3rd or 4th of March, but sometimes the orders were not carried out in full, and for some reason, a number of soldiers would be kept by the unit where they were trained so that units in Kosovo were not really replenished to capacity. If just a few specialised soldiers failed to arrive, such as a tank driver or a person in charge of aiming, that was a huge problem. There was another problem. There were forces of the UNPROFOR and international forces in Macedonia monitoring the region, and they had withdrawn. As soon as they withdrew, their positions were taken over by NATO. To us it was a sure sign that the aggression was going to start shortly and it was a problem, because we had to expect now terrorist forces in areas which they had not occupied before. And in case of land invasion, we expected the terrorists to be the advance units in the invasion. And thirdly, we were saving our assets, and I asked that reserve troops not be kept on rotation longer than they were supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every strategic grouping had a prescribed level of troops from the reserve. Why did we use reserve men? Because we didn't have enough. In those circumstances, it was allowed for a certain number of reservists to be kept within units. If that number was exceeded, we had to react through our section for recruitment and mobilisation, and we had to release them because otherwise there would be a shortage of materiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suppose it's time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Djurdjic. We will have the normal break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you briefly tell us what measures of combat-readiness means?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Combat-readiness measures indicate the status of the army as a whole or some of its parts in terms of their readiness for response or reaction to implement tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there some sort of grade there, and what does that depend on?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, there are grades. There are differences between full combat-readiness where the unit is ready immediately to set out its assignments. Then there is a three-hour, six-hour, 24-hour, and even longer level of readiness and that depends on the degree of possible surprise and the need to take measures to prevent this surprise from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P965, please. This is a meeting of the General Staff collegium of the 11th of March, 1999. Can we look at page 12 in the English and page 11 -- sorry, page 11 in the English and page 11 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And in your binder, General, that would be binder -- that would be page 10. At the top of the page I'm interested in the first and third paragraphs. In the English it would be paragraph 3 on page 11, the end of page 11 and top of page 12. Can you please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I remember very well this situation and this address of mine to the collegium because this situation at the border between Macedonia and Serbia had become more complex and Albania and Serbia as well, in Kosovo, that border. And there was the risk of a surprise action after the control of the state border between Macedonia and Serbia was taken over by NATO. The command of the 3rd Army was permitted by the Chief of the General Staff to use the peacetime composition of the 37th Motorised Brigade from the 2nd Army, from the Raska Garrison to be relocated to Kosovska Mitrovica. That was a force of 325 men, officers, non-commissioned officers, and regular soldiers. It was also planned for the 21st Combat Group, which was located in Nis, a force of some 70 to 80 men, to be brought to Kosovo and Metohija and to have them resubordinated in Urosevac to the 234th Motorised Brigade of the Pristina Corps because those sectors were extremely sensitive and vulnerable. I've already said that there was the chance of surprise action, a surprise attack, and in order to forestall this and fully aware of all the facts, the Chief of the General Staff ordered this to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this done secretly?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, it was announced to the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask for the next paragraph. If you could explain that to me regarding this subordination of the second and third groups to the Nis Corps. Did that have to do anything with the sending of recruits?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. In the last session I explained that the Chief of the General Staff ordered for young soldiers, recruits, not to be trained in the endangered area in Kosovo and Metohija until their training was completed. That is why part of the 1st and the 2nd Army, the navy, the recruits who were mobilised were trained; and then pursuant to the order and the plan of the General Staff and with the announcement to the adequate OSCE mission, were only then sent by train to the Kosovo and Metohija area. We did have certain difficulties there, as you can see, not the full number of reservists left, only 476 soldiers, less than ordered, were actually dispatched. This had to be corrected later. Some soldiers in the meantime were unfit to serve, some got sick, sustained various types of injuries, they were in the hospital, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the next paragraph regarding this broadening of the border area, could you clarify that? Could you tell us a little bit more about that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I've already said that the department for border services, which was part of the first administration made an estimate, and based on the request by the 3rd Army the situation in the General Staff was analysed. And the Chief of the General Staff received a recommendation and was asked to make an order via the Federal Ministry of Defence and the federal government to move the border area and make this border sector a bit broader, on our side of the border in the event of certain incidents, because those guarding the border were allowed to act only within our territory, on our side of the border. And this is why we suggested - and I'm reporting here that the federal government permitted - this broadening of the border area. This is a colloquial term, the expansion of the border area. This is a set border area established by the federal government, and this was published in the Official Gazette. After that, it was passed down to the lower levels and the population was then informed about this and boards were posted that the border sector was expanded, its specific areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We will go into more detail about this with our following witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look at page 21 of the English version now, please, and in your document it is page 18, General. And in the Serbian it is page 19 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We can see at the end of the page here the address by the Chief of the General Staff, Mr. Ojdanic, and I would like to ask you to comment what he says here regarding his conversation with Clark.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The Chief of the General Staff at one point at this collegium informed us about this conversation which was conducted by telephone in his office. What this is about, General Clark called General Ojdanic, and he was angry with him and wanted to speak with him. Actually I think - and this was also the assessment by General Ojdanic - that the most important thing for him was to threaten us and to exert pressure on General Ojdanic, for him to persuade the state leadership to act the way NATO wanted them to act, and this is what happened at that time. Nothing was said by General Clark in that conversation about refugees or humanitarian catastrophe or anything like that. He was allegedly concerned because there was a brigade numbering 25.000 people at the edge of Kosovo and Metohija. I responded that we never had a brigade of 25.000 people anywhere, perhaps 205 -- 2.500-strong. Yes. There was no agreement, however, limiting us or restricting us from having forces outside of Kosovo and Metohija territory, at the outskirts or the edge of Kosovo and Metohija. That time General Clark had received a report that we had brought a part of the 37th Motorised Brigade from the Raska Garrison, and the 21st Combat Group to the Kosovo and Metohija area. I recall that in that conversation General Ojdanic very seriously stated that we cannot sit with our hands in our laps in Belgrade and wait for somebody to attack us or not attack us at the same time as they were bringing in a considerable force. At that time they had 9.500 men in Macedonia prepared to move to implement assignments in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just this, sir, according to our rules and regulations, how much can a military brigade -- how many men it can have at the maximum?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, depending on its nature, whether it's an infantry brigade, anti-aircraft, a full-strength brigade can number from 2.000 to 4.000 men. Infantry and motorised brigade would be the biggest, while the armoured brigades would be the smallest because they have small crews and teams depending on the number of tanks and so on, they number much less. But it can go up to 2.500 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D006-0392, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is an order by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and it's in tab 11 in your -- in your binder and the date is the 16th of March, 1999. Can you briefly explain this order and the main assignment in this order being issued to the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: After a visit to the 3rd Army and inspecting the units of the 3rd Army, primarily of the Pristina Corps on the 3rd and 4th of March, 1999, and in order to resolve some problems that had cropped up, we are writing an order because we were part of that team. The basic purpose of this order was to undertake measures to prevent any surprise actions, as you can see in the first key paragraphs, 1 and 2, of this order, the primary task is to secure the state borders. And it says: "The main mission of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps is to continue to secure the state borders of the FRY towards Albania and Macedonia," and that is where you see very clearly what the long-term assignment is for the 3rd Army command. In terms of the forces that had been brought -- that NATO had brought forward from the rear, it was essential again to evaluate whether the forces allocated to secure the state border was sufficient. Besides that, it was essential to make more detailed assessments about the required quantities of ammunition, food, fuels, medical supplies, and other supplies in order to enable the border forces to act independently and self-sufficiently. They are acting in remote areas, inaccessible for immediate aid and assistance, so they are required to be self-sufficient. So this is then a special assignment that is being issued to them for the longer term because they need to take specific measures in the event of being exposed to an attack. There are many items in this order --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. We can read for ourselves what the other items of this order contain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit Number D00559. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D006-0447, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is tab 12 in your binder, General, and it's number 42 ter among the Defence documents. And this is a caution or a warning of the first administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia of the 20th of March, 1999. There is a warning here. We can see that. Can you please tell us who drafted the document, to whom was it addressed.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. Pursuant to the order by the Chief of the General Staff, I personally drafted this document on behalf of the administration. This was a warning to the 3rd Army; however, it was sent for purposes of information to others. This is a telegram. Please take note of the date, it is the 20th of March, only four days before the NATO aggression on our country began; and the General Staff - knowing that a provocation could take place from any side, either from the Siptar terrorist forces or the NATO forces in the territory of Macedonia or a provocation by our soldiers against the NATO forces, so in order to avoid such a possible situation and with the intention of not allowing some individual incident to serve as a pretext or a cause and to provoke NATO action against our country, I am writing a detailed order here, warning how to behave and how to avoid anything like that. You can see that it's a telegram and the encryption officer wrote on the original what time the telegram was dispatched. And then you can see that it was sent at 1510 hours to the 2nd Army, 1520 hours to the 3rd Army, 1545 to the air force and so on. And then there are the initials of the dispatcher, the signature and stamp of the Chief of the General Staff, and what is below is when the telegram was received, when it was processed, and when it was sent on. Received it means received at the encryption office, then when it was processed, then when it was delivered, and this is at 1620 hours to the last unit. We also have a stamp and a date in order to avoid any eventuality of forgeries or changes being made to this information. That's it in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as D00560. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document D006-0385, please. This is a warning by the Supreme Command Staff of the 25th of March, 1999 -- I apologise. I did make an error. No, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir. General, sir, will you please tell us what this warning is, who drafted it. This is tab 14 in your binder, sir. This is the 65 ter Defence document 35.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Of the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Evidently this is a telegram encrypted and sent to all the commands of the strategic groups and others who were in communication with the General Staff and obliged to send regular reports. In peacetime this was the daily operations report of the 24th of March. From the 24th of March these became combat reports because they were drafted during combat. This was dispatched by the first administration in order to submit correct and confirmed reports, please undertake the following measures, namely, we had not been in a war for over 50 years and we did not have fresh combat experience, such as other countries might have. So for us it was the first day of the war from the 24th to the 25th of March it was an important day for us, and it was a surprise. So perhaps at some lower levels individuals did not quite find their way, and that's why it was necessary to warn them that they needed to provide correct and verified data about what was going on in the units, and in particular in relation to the NATO bombing and the effects of that bombing because we should not be in a position to operate on the basis of unverified and incorrect information because NATO knew precisely which targets it was striking. And this is why the warning was issued for the commanders to do their utmost to provide absolutely accurate and precise data.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit Number D00561. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D006-2663, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is 491 in the Defence 65 ter, and this is tab 15, General, in your binder. This document has now been tendered. Can we now have D008-2663. I'm sorry if I made this error. This is a combat report of the 3rd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The combat report of the 3rd of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, just one moment. Let's wait until it appears on the screen. Yes, this is it. This is a combat report. General, so I would just like us to explain a few things here. First of all, can you please tell us what is a combat report?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: A combat report is a summary of all the information that arrived via regular channels in writing from subordinate units to the Supreme Command Staff, and all this information would contain all that is important or of interest for the collegium, for the Supreme Command Staff, and for the headquarters and the Supreme Command. It's written once every day. So we have report number 10 here, so it means that up until that day nine previous reports were drafted and sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you correctly, who sends this information on the basis of which the summary report is written?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: A combat report to the Supreme Command Staff is written on the basis of same such combat reports received from commands of the strategic groups and independent units that are directly reporting to the General Staff, meaning that each army would send a combat report by a certain dead-line and they in turn would receive such reports from the corps or brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did you draft the report of the staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: The combat report would be drafted by the duty operations team headed by a general. The team had a certain number of persons, colonels from all the organisational units. Most of them came from the first administration because it was their job to process this information, but there were also representatives of the navy, the air force, logistics, security, morale, from all the organisational units because they had to provide their contribution to the combat report after having studied all the reports from the strategic groups that had been received so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be able to tell us how reports received from the 3rd Army were processed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Reports from the 3rd Army were processed in the same way as reports from other strategic formations, but there was some additional care in their case because the bulk of the activities took place there, most of the problems were there, and the most complex situation for the country was in that location. So the 3rd Army report was studied more carefully. They were studied by the desk officers for the 3rd Army and by all the other members of the team. And all the most important data that would come, just like that contained in other combat reports, had to be put into this report that was sent to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's page 3 for you too, point 2.4, Overview of the activities of the 3rd Army according to attachment number 1.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This was a case when all the commands of strategic groups submitted their reports in good time, but for some technical reason because of a breakdown in communications or for some other reason there was a serious delay in receiving the reports of the 3rd Army. The person who signed the reports therefore decided that several hours later when the report finally arrived it would be produced in an attachment and processed properly by 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me about these reports coming in from strategic groups. What were the most important parts of these reports?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Situation in the territory, situation in the units, losses suffered from NATO bombing, and changes in the area, where the new units of the aggressor came in, whether a new aircraft carrier arrived or a new helicopter carrier. At some point we received a report that another 200 cruise missiles were delivered, things that were relevant to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, these reports from strategic groups, specifically the 3rd Army, did they have to also reflect problems that occurred in the command and reports of crimes committed on that day in the area of responsibility of the army that they were aware of?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Certainly. Several paragraphs of such a report had to contain this, passages related to security because it is the security organs that would write this paragraph, problems in command, state of morale, and conclusions. All important information, developments, and problems had to be reflected in the report. If such things did not fit into any particular paragraph, they could be described at the end, in a separate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, I see that you signed the report that day. Was it the case every day, that you as chief of section would -- chief of department would sign?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. Every day the operations duty team monitoring the situation would rotate and make a report in the evening. On this day I was the chief of the duty operations team, and I described everything received in the reports by strategic groups. I see my desk officer wrote this, Milivoj Gutovic, we see the name of the typist, and the names of the addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's what I want to know. This was done in seven copies and submitted to whom?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: We were well-trained professionals. We strictly observed the procedure, and every original indicated to whom each copy was delivered. Of course copy number 1 went to files. The second copy to the supreme commander. Every morning by 6.00 a.m. the head of the duty operations team make sure that the military office of the supreme commander should receive this report by courier in an envelope. You see that copy number 3 was delivered to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff; copy number 4 to the federal defence minister; copy number 5 to the president of the Republic of Serbia, as member of the Supreme Defence Council; the sixth copy to the deputy Chief of the General Staff, because he was not always in the same location for security reasons; and copy number 7 stayed and was kept by the shift leader, so he could use it if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask that this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit Number D00562. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about the purpose of these combat reports received by the Supreme Command Staff and those outgoing. It's obviously a case of reporting up and down the chain, but I want to know this: If there were certain problems emphasized in the reports from subordinate units within a strategic group, what would be the reaction of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, that depends on the problem, the scale of the problem, the urgency. The Supreme Command Staff would react in various ways. Sometimes they didn't even have to wait for the regular combat report. If problems were familiar to the head of the team, he would immediately inform the supreme commander if necessary. If the problem was of a different nature, then it would be notified to the body concerned. If it was a logistical matter, then it would be addressed to the chief of logistics; if it was a question of morale, then to the chief of the section for morale; if it was a security issue, then it would be notified to the chief of security. Other matters would be referred to the section for operation and staff affairs for their consideration and further action.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document, an individual combat report from the Supreme Command Staff, is not something I want to tender. With the assistance of Mr. Stamp, we made a list of all reports of the Supreme Command Staff and some reports from the command of the 3rd Army; and with the consent of Mr. Stamp, we would like to submit this list to the Trial Chamber for later admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that mean you contemplate that you will tender these reports at a later date by consent? Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I believe it's much more efficient than tendering them one by one. Could we now see D006-0451.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is 30th May 1999, Supreme Command Staff instructions for writing combat reports. What were the reasons why this instruction was drafted?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, war is war. All kinds of things happen in war: Breakdown in communications, overburdened communications, relocation of command posts for security reasons. There came a time when we found ourselves in a situation when the chief of the Supreme Command Staff was not quite satisfied with the breadth and the precision of certain requests. In addition, certain commands, especially at lower levels, did not fully observe the earlier instructions for drafting reports. And at that point, he ordered a new instruction to be made and to add new content so that the Supreme Command Staff would have a complete picture of the situation, and thus be able to provide appropriate reports to the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.8 is what I want to ask you about, situation in the territory, attachment number 1.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: As you can see just by glancing through the contents, this lists various points of the combat report, who - which command produced them - the time when it was drafted and bullet points. In 2.8 you see that the operative administration on duty, in the duty team, has to produce this paragraph by 1.00, and it has to contain a summarised overview of NATO activities, protest gatherings, epidemics, floods, important events relevant to the VJ, and conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see point 3.3. That's on the next page in Serbian and the English is still okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Next page for you.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Point 3 was within the jurisdiction of the recruitment, mobilisation, and system issues department because the Chief of the General Staff had ordered that every day within combat reports he wanted to receive information about the work of the judiciary. The judiciary was not under the Chief of the General Staff because the judges were independent, but what he required was to know the number of criminal reports filed, the number of indictees, and the number of sanctions pronounced every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And number 4?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: This was within the jurisdiction of the department for morale, and we again see bullet points of topics that needed to be covered in the report, confidence in the Supreme Command --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We can read that. What about point 5?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Point 5 was at our level written by the security administration and at lower levels by security organs. Again, you see bullet points covering content that must be reflected in every report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Under which point would we find that -- the security situation in your report to the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: I would have to take a look at the report. It was not always the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you about the previous period. This was supposed to take effect on the 30th of May, but before the 30th of May, under what point was the security situation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, it's not so important under which number it was, but there was always a separate paragraph listing all relevant information. We can go back to one of the combat reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 15.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN
